title: 1-Chloropropane and AlCl₃: a hydride shift
subtitle: The primary cation never forms: H shifts as chloride leaves

reactants.caption: 1-chloropropane + aluminium chloride
reactants.learnerPrompt: Aluminium chloride is a Lewis acid. Show it binding to the alkyl chloride.
hintTiers: Which atom of AlCl₃ is electron-poor? Which atom of the alkyl chloride has lone pairs?
The chlorine uses a lone pair to bond to aluminium. One arrow.
Cl5 lone pair → new Cl5–Al7 bond.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: A primary alkyl chloride does not ionise on its own. Let the Lewis acid take a lone pair first.

complex.caption: alkyl chloride–AlCl₃ complex
complex.learnerPrompt: Chloride leaves as AlCl₄⁻, but a primary carbocation is too unstable to form. What happens at the same time?
hintTiers: A primary carbocation is never formed. Which neighbouring bond can move in as the C–Cl bond breaks?
The C–Cl bond breaks onto chlorine while the C–H bond on the middle carbon carries its H across to the end carbon (a 1,2-hydride shift). Two arrows.
σ C4–Cl5 → lone pair on Cl5; σ C2–H3 → new bond C4–H3 (point at the dashed line).

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Chloride leaves, but that would leave a primary carbocation. Let a hydride shift in from the neighbouring carbon at the same time.

steps.explanationAfterStep: The chlorine, now bonded to aluminium, is positively charged: a much better leaving group.
The secondary cation is much more stable than a primary one (hyperconjugation from two methyl groups).

mechanismSummary: AlCl₃ binds the chlorine. As chloride leaves, a hydride shifts from the neighbouring carbon, so a primary carbocation is never formed: the product is the secondary, isopropyl cation. This is why Friedel–Crafts alkylation with 1-chloropropane gives isopropylbenzene, not propylbenzene.
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 21
